newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prosecutors raid homes of former Nomura heads.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors raid homes of former Nomura heads.

text.p: Prosecutors raided the homes of former Nomura Securities chairman Setsuya Tabuchi and former president Yoshihisa Tabuchi (no relation) on Friday in a widening probe over a payoff scandal, Japanese media reported.
The latest raid follows the arrests earlier this week of three former Nomura executives and a racketeer in a case that has linked the firm to corporate extortionists.
The two Tabuchis resigned in 1991 after similar revelations that the top brokerage firm compensated elite clients for losses and that affiliates dealt with organised crime.

But they both rejoined Nomura's board in 1995, triggering a controversy among Nomura employees because the two were regarded as symbols of the firm's old reputation for aggressively grabbing profits at the expense of small investors' interests.
Nomura said it could not immediately confirm the raids on the Tabuchi homes and that it was checking with prosecutors.

On Wednesday, the Tokyo District Prosecutors' Office said Ryuichi Koike was arrested on suspicion of taking 50 million yen ($431,000) in illegal payments from Nomura to stop him from disrupting the company's 1995 annual shareholders' meeting.

The Securities and Exchange Law and the Commercial Code ban brokerages from making payments to "sokaiya" and compensating clients for investment losses. The laws also forbid firms from conducting discretionary stock transactions.
Koike's younger brother, a realtor, was also arrested on suspicion of being an accomplice in the affair by allowing his company to be a front for payment of the money.
The racketeers, known as "sokaiya", extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.

Former Nomura managing directors Shimpei Matsuki and Nobutaka Fujikura, and Osamu Fujita, a general affairs officer in charge of shareholder meetings, were also arrested this week for their suspected involvement in the payoffs to Koike.
Since the scandal broke in March, Nomura's president and 15 board members have resigned to accept management responsibility for the scandal.
At the heart of the investigation is whether the firm's executive board was aware of the payoffs to Koike or whether the officials involved acted on their own.
